title: Citation sanctions: Plausible arguments cannot excuse fabrication
desc: Maintains counsel’s verification duty and considers deterrence, fee shifting and client accountability, while separating tentative sanctions from professional reporting.

kps.k: AI-assisted research leaves counsel responsible for verifying the authorities they submit.
kps.d: In Lacey v. State Farm General Ins. Co., the special master relies on counsel’s declarations to attribute fake or inaccurate authorities in a privilege brief to Copeland’s use of several AI tools. He accepts Copeland’s admission of responsibility and invokes Rule 11’s reasonable-inquiry requirement. The episode illustrates accountability for unchecked AI output, not a measured hallucination rate or evidence that all legal AI use is improper.

kps.k: Plausible legal arguments do not resolve the separate problem of fabricated supporting authorities.
kps.d: Counsel contend that the brief’s underlying privilege principles were likely legitimate; the special master records that contention without independently endorsing it. He nevertheless condemns the research practices and says the filing weakened his confidence in all of plaintiff’s counsel’s factual and legal assertions. The practical risk therefore extends beyond correcting individual citations to losing credibility across the litigation.

kps.k: The proposed response combines deterrence, expense shifting and client accountability rather than treating the incident solely as a technical error.
kps.d: The special master identifies defense attorney fees and special-master costs associated with the privilege dispute and invokes the appointment order and Rules 11 and 37. Tentative measures include joint and several liability for Ellis George and K&L Gates for special-master fees related to the bogus briefs and show-cause proceedings, plus written notice from Copeland to his client about the proceedings’ substance and outcome. These proposals place consequences at both lawyer and firm level. References to striking pleadings or restricting claims describe available Rule 37 measures, not established selections here.

kps.k: The excerpts describe a tentative, contestable outcome and distinguish fee awards from professional-reporting consequences.
kps.d: Despite the source title’s reference to sanctions, the special master gives counsel an opportunity to respond and attend a hearing before final resolution. He prohibits AI only for the specified response, which may not exceed five pages; this does not establish a general ban on AI-assisted practice. He also expresses his legal view, citing Medina, that a Rule 37 fee award should not count as a personal sanction potentially reportable to the California State Bar. The record therefore requires distinctions between proposed and final sanctions, case-specific restrictions and general rules, and financial liability and disciplinary reporting.

vlens.an: The court and regulatory voice represented here supports the proposition that counsel’s verification duty is unchanged by AI assistance and that plausible underlying legal principles cannot excuse fabricated authorities. The special master treats the filing as counsel’s responsibility, links the response to reasonable inquiry, deterrence and costs caused, and contemplates both firm-level fee liability and client notice. Material qualification does not weaken that support: the measures described were tentative and contestable, the prohibition on AI was limited to the response to the notice rather than framed as a general ban, and the special master distinguished a Rule 37 fee award from a potentially reportable personal sanction. Because the curated evidence contains one judicial source, this establishes that source’s position rather than the prevalence of this view among regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that counsel’s verification duty persists when using AI and that plausible underlying legal arguments do not excuse fabricated authorities. Its reasoning links unchecked AI-assisted research to counsel’s responsibility for filed submissions, loss of credibility extending beyond the defective citations, actual litigation costs, and the need for a measured deterrent response through fee shifting and client notice. Material internal variation concerns the form and procedural status of the consequences, not the core duty: the measures described were tentative and contestable; the prohibition on AI applied to the specified response rather than legal practice generally; and the special master distinguished a Rule 37 fee award from a personally reportable professional sanction. Because the curated evidence contains one case-specific source, it establishes this source’s position rather than the prevalence of that view in 2025 or the state of adoption at scale generally.

parents.t: Professional-work evidence: Role structure and study design bound claims about AI effects

sources.t: Lacey v. State Farm General Ins. Co. — Special Master Order Sanctioning Ellis George and K&L Gates for AI-Generated Fake Citations
